messages.subject: Making a Simple World Map to Show Site on a Desired Latitude
messages.subject_clean: Making a Simple World Map to Show Site on a Desired Latitude
messages.body_plain:
Dear D-RUGgies,

I'm making a simple world map to show some sampling sites, but I've been having trouble with 1) centering the map in the desired location, 2) changing the projection of the map to best show areas, distances, and shapes.

My goal is to simply display a number of Northern Hemisphere coastal sites on a single map that shows uninterrupted ocean basins (normally, map() in the maps package would cut the Pacific Ocean in half).

I would greatly appreciate any suggestions that can help me make a prettier map.

Below is the code I use to make the attached map figure.

Thank you very much,

Matt

#-----------------------------------------------------------------------
library( maps )

# function that will plot a world map centered on a desired longitude
plot.map<- function(database,center,...){
    Obj <- map(database,...,plot=F)
    coord <- cbind(Obj[[1]],Obj[[2]])

    # split up the coordinates
    id <- rle(!is.na <http://is.na>(coord[,1]))
    id <- matrix(c(1,cumsum(id$lengths)),ncol=2,byrow=T)
    polygons <- apply(id,1,function(i){coord[i[1]:i[2],]})

    # split up polygons that differ too much
    polygons <- lapply(polygons,function(x){
        x[,1] <- x[,1] + center
        x[,1] <- ifelse(x[,1]>180,x[,1]-360,x[,1])
        if(sum(diff(x[,1])>300,na.rm=T) >0){
          id <- x[,1] < 0
          x <- rbind(x[id,],c(NA,NA),x[!id,])
       }
       x
    })
    # reconstruct the object
    polygons <- do.call(rbind,polygons)
    Obj[[1]] <- polygons[,1]
    Obj[[2]] <- polygons[,2]

    map(Obj,...)
}

# Site information: codes, geographic locations
Sites <- c('AK','BB','BC','FI','JN','JS','MA','NC','NN','PO','QU','SD','SW','VA','WA')
Lats  <- c(59.648,38.317,49.000,60.100,43.060,34.178,42.426,34.683,67.233,36.997,49.113,32.714,58.314,37.217,46.500)
Longs <- c(-151.436,-123.033,-123.100,21.700, 144.911-360,132.550-360,  # Note, Japanese site had to be adjusted by 360 degrees to work with "maps" package
          -70.919,-76.600,15.200,-7.829,-68.179,-117.226, 11.548,-76.383,-124.000)
# Colors for Atlantic (blue) and Pacific (green) sites
Cols  = c(rep('green',3),'blue',rep('green',2),rep('blue',5),'green',rep('blue',2),'green')
# Adjustments for site code text, so they can be offset slightly from actual locations
Adjx  <- c( -0.5,1.5,-0.5,-0.5,-0.5,-0.5,-0.5,-0.5,1.5,1.5,1.5,1.5,1.5,-0.5,1.5 )
Adjy  <- c(  1.2,0.5,-0.5,-0.5, 0.5, 1.2, 0.8, 0.7,0.5,0.5,0.5,  1,1.2, 0.3,0.5 )

# Wrap Site info into a data.frame
SiteList <- data.frame( site=Sites, lat=Lats, long=Longs, cols=Cols, adjx=Adjx, adjy=Adjy )
# coerce colors into a character vector because default is factor
SiteList$cols <- as.character( SiteList$cols )

# Plot World Map, use "center=" to change the central longitude of the projection
windows(12,5)
center <- 60
plot.map("world", center=center, col="moccasin",bg="skyblue",
   fill=TRUE, ylim=c(20,85), mar=c(4,7,0,0) )

# Add Points at Site Locations. Note, have to add "center" amount to longitude to correct for map adjustment
with(SiteList, points( long+center, lat, pch=21, col=1, bg=cols, cex=1.8 ))
# Add Site labels using a for loop so each label can be adjusted by the amount specified in SiteList
for(i in 1:nrow(SiteList)){
     with(SiteList[i,], text( long+center, lat, labels=site, adj=c(adjx,adjy), cex=0.8, font=2 ))
}
#-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Department of Evolution & Ecology
University of California, Davis

Hi, I'm very new to the forum, and I apologize in advance for asking a total "newby" question straight out of the gate.  I've been working with R and R studio for about a year, but I'm just now starting to work with larger data sets.

I'm working with 16 text files that total 9GB.  Together they contain about 16 million records with between 50 and 120 variables for each record.  Of course, when I attempt to open this in R studio, it says I'm way over the limit.  I'm baffled because R is supposed to be THE big data resource.  Should I look into R Revolution Analytic?  If so, any advice on getting started?  Would another stat's program, like SAS or STATA, be more appropriate?  I'm not doing anything particularly sophisticated with the data, just counts and rates really.  I've just never worked with something so big before.

Thank so much for your patience and advice!

Mallory

PS, I'm working on a PC, 64-bit, Intel Core i5-4200U with 8GB installed memory.

PSS, I signed up for the Data Carpentry workshop through VetMed later this month.  A giant THANK YOU for posting.  I cannot tell you how timely and helpful it is.

messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: Large Data Sets / R Revolution Analytics
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mallory,

Vince beat me to the punch.  Since your data files (9GB) exceed your computer's memory (8GB), you'll need some approach that either reduces the data or can deal with it without reading it into memory.  A Vince suggests, dealing with the files in turn might be useful.

For a database approach, you can use the RSQLite package to convert the *.csv files into a database, as described here: http://stackoverflow.com/a/12392189/1757441. Then you can connect to the database using the dplyr package, and use all its commands to manipulate the data as described here: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dplyr/vignettes/databases.html

Revolution Analytics' version of R is designed for data and computations that are spread across many computers, so probably would not be applicable in your case.

Big data material like this won't be specifically covered at the Data Carpentry workshop, but if you drop by a Friday work session we can work through options.

Noam

Didn't have much time to look at this but might be worth looking into using the ggvis or ggmap functions...you'll probably have to play around with this a bit more to make it look as you'd like but just as a demo (sitelist is equivalent to your SiteList dataframe):

library(googleVis)
library(ggmap)
library(maps)

## GGMAP
al1<-get_map(location = 'U.S.', zoom = 3, maptype = "terrain")
map<-ggmap(al1)

# prob need to tweak this a bit
map+geom_point(data=sitelist, aes(x=long, y=lat), color="maroon", pch=16, size=6)+
  geom_text(data=sitelist, aes(x=(long-adjx), y=(lat-adjy), label=site))

## Another option it takes a sec to load
library(OpenStreetMap)
map <- openmap(c(60,-179), c(-60,179),zoom=3)
map <- openproj(map)

autoplot(map) + #geom_point(aes(x=reclong,y=reclat))
  geom_point(data=sitelist, aes(x=long, y=lat), color="maroon", pch=16, size=6)

## A NICE WORLDMAP
world <- map_data("world")
worldmap <- ggplot(world, aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group)) +
  geom_path() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=(-2:2) * 30) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=(-4:4) * 45)

worldmap + coord_map("ortho")

Hope this might be helpful!,
Adios,
Ryan

Hi,

I'm trying to parallelize code for iteratively extracting values from individual bands of a multi-band temperature raster at a set of points. Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
  3 nodes produced errors; first error: Error in open.ncdf trying to open file C:\Users\DYoung\R\multithread_extract\tmax_1998.nc <http://tmax_1998.nc>

I believe this is because even once loaded, RasterLayer objects simply reference files until used in operations (is this right?) and the nodes are not able to access my computer's file system (is this also right?).

If this indeed what is happening, is there any way to make the nodes able to access my computer's file system? Or is there some other potential solution?

I have attached sample code that replicates this problem. You can download the multi-band raster it uses here  <https://www.dropbox.com/s/dlzghy5hs0vr01b/tmax_1998.nc?dl=0>(150 MB).

Thanks in advance,
Derek

Dear Davis R Users Group!

I'm having a problem with (I think) the way two tables are being read into R. Hi Catherine,

First off — I'm not familiar with these particular packages, so I can't help you entirely there. But, I tried to replicate the issue and found this:

> obs.null.output<-cbind(dbFD(traits[colnames(my.sample),],my.sample)$FDis,replicate(9,dbfd.shuff(traits)))
Error in dbFD(traits[colnames(my.sample), ], my.sample) :
  'x' must have names.

x is the first argument, and you've provided it a vector. This is a subtly of R: when accessing a single column, R will return a vector, not a dataframe of one column. You can prevent R from dropping these other dimensions by setting drop=FALSE in the bracket operator:

> dbFD(traits[colnames(my.sample),, drop=FALSE],my.sample)
FRic: Only one continuous trait or dimension in 'x'. FRic was measured as the range, NOT as the convex hull volume.
FDiv: Cannot not be computed when 'x' contains one single continuous trait or dimension.

Ok, that worked — let's make the same change to your function:

dbfd.shuff<-function(x)
{
  rownames(x)<-sample(rownames(x),length(rownames(x)),replace=F)
  dbFD(x[colnames(my.sample),, drop=FALSE],my.sample)$FDis
}

Now test it:

> obs.null.output<-cbind(dbFD(traits[colnames(my.sample),, drop=FALSE],my.sample)$FDis,replicate(9,dbfd.shuff(traits)))

Actually, I think I may understand what you mean. I've created a dataframe of some random letters that is analogous to your diagnosis columns. You want to subset to keep rows where any of some columns (all in this example) where any of these columns has that value. So:

> # make fake data
> d <- data.frame(x1=sample(letters[1:10], 10, replace=TRUE),
                            x2=sample(letters[1:10], 10, replace=TRUE),
                            x3=sample(letters[1:10], 10, replace=TRUE))

> vec <- c('a', 'c', 'g') # vector of keep (e.g. your septicemia)
> lapply(d, function(x) x %in% vec) # loop across columns, indicating which entries are in vec
$x1
 [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

$x2
 [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

$x3
 [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
> do.call(cbind, lapply(d, function(x) x %in% vec))  # bind these all up into a dataframe
         x1    x2    x3
 [1,]  TRUE FALSE FALSE
 [2,] FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [3,]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
 [4,] FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [5,] FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [6,] FALSE FALSE FALSE
 [7,] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
 [8,]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE
 [9,] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
[10,] FALSE FALSE FALSE
> apply(do.call(cbind, lapply(d, function(x) x %in% vec)), 1, any)  # now, if any of col's values in vec, keep
 [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

Now you have an indexing vector:

> i <- apply(do.call(cbind, lapply(d, function(x) x %in% vec)), 1, any)
> d[i, ]
  x1 x2 x3
1  c  e  j
3  g  g  a
7  j  c  e
8  a  e  g
9  i  a  c

You may need to coerce your data.table to a data.frame, but this is the idea. I think there might be a simpler way, but this is a good first approximation to get the problem solved and move forward.

Of course you don't need to do the whole lapply() stuff — you could do this by writing out all the logical comparisons, but I don't like tedious things like that.

Hope this helps,
V

I thought about using apply() directly as you did, but I think in general it's wise to try to avoid it. apply() will always coerce any non-array object with dimensions (e.g. a dataframe) to a matrix using as.matrix() first — and I try to avoid as many implicit coercions as possible (I've been bitten in the past by this). But in this case, as.matrix() on these columns will return a character vector matrix so it should be safe (but maybe not a good general approach).

This approach would be faster (if speed is an issue). Using any() rather than sum() should be faster (I believe any() short circuit evaluates — anyone know for sure?).

Vince
